questions.question: What is the most characteristic peak age for presenting acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is more common in children aged 2 to 6 years, although it can occur in schoolchildren, but the maximum peak is in preschool age.

questions.question: What age group has the highest incidence of acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: The peak incidence of acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is observed in preschoolers aged 2 to 6 years, being rare in infants and newborns.

questions.question: In what age range is the diagnosis of acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis most typical?
questions.explanation: Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis has its maximum peak between 2 and 6 years, being less frequent at extreme ages of childhood.

questions.question: What is the most common clinical presentation in a 4-year-old child with acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
options: Low back pain and high fever
questions.explanation: In a preschooler with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, the classic triad includes gross hematuria, edema, and arterial hypertension, not polyuria or lower urinary symptoms.

questions.question: What infectious history is most relevant in a 3-year-old child with acute glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is caused by nephritogenic strains of group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus, not other common pathogens.

questions.question: What is the initial first-line management in a 5-year-old child with acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis and arterial hypertension?
questions.explanation: Initial treatment includes eradication of streptococcus with antibiotics and management of hypertension with antihypertensives, reserving diuretics for significant edema.

questions.question: What is the typical latency period between streptococcal infection and the onset of acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis has a latency period of 1 to 3 weeks after pharyngeal or skin infection, the time necessary for the formation of immune complexes and their glomerular deposition.

questions.question: What differentiates poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis from rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis in terms of its temporal course?
questions.explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis occurs with a latency of 1 to 3 weeks, while the rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis usually manifests in days or weeks and with accelerated deterioration; Latency is a key data to differentiate them.

questions.question: What is the main pathophysiological mechanism of acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune complex glomerulonephritis: antigen-antibody complexes are deposited in the glomerulus, activating complement and triggering inflammation, with a latency of 1 to 3 weeks.

questions.question: What clinical finding is characteristic of the onset of acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis after the latency period?
questions.explanation: After the latency of 1-3 weeks, hematuria (choluric urine), edema, hypertension and oliguria classically appear; Fever and arthralgia are more typical of the infectious phase, not the onset of nephritis.

questions.question: What complementary study confirms streptococcal etiology in a patient with acute glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Elevation of antistreptolysin O (ASO) or other antistreptococcal enzymes evidences recent streptococcal infection, supporting the diagnosis of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis; ANA and IgA point to other etiologies.

questions.question: What is the initial supportive treatment in acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis during the acute phase?
questions.explanation: Initial management is supportive: rest, sodium and fluid restriction, diuretics for edema and antihypertensives; Corticosteroids and immunosuppressants are not indicated in the typical post-streptococcal form.

questions.question: In acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, the typical complement pattern is:
questions.explanation: Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is characterized by activation of the alternative complement pathway, which produces C3 consumption with normal C4, unlike other glomerulonephritis that presents with low C4 due to activation of the classic pathway.

questions.question: Which complement pathway is activated in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis mainly activates the alternative complement pathway, which explains the isolated decrease in C3 with preserved C4, unlike the classic pathway that consumes both components.

questions.question: What immunopathological finding is observed in the renal biopsy of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis presents granular deposits of C3 in immunofluorescence, along with IgG to a lesser extent, reflecting the deposition of immune complexes and the activation of the alternative complement pathway.

questions.question: What is the main supportive treatment in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is usually self-limiting; Management is supportive with hypertension control, diuretics for volume overload and sodium restriction, without indication for steroids or immunosuppressants in most cases.

questions.question: What renal sequelae is most common in children after poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: In the pediatric population, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis has an excellent prognosis: the vast majority present complete recovery of renal function, with resolution of hematuria and proteinuria in weeks to months.

questions.question: Which laboratory indicator supports the diagnosis of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis is supported by evidence of recent streptococcal infection (elevated ASO) together with hypocomplementemia of C3 with normal C4, a typical pattern of the alternating pathway, which helps differentiate it from other glomerulonephritis.

questions.question: What pathophysiological mechanism explains acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is a disease mediated by immune complexes that are deposited in the glomerulus, activating complement and causing kidney damage.

questions.question: Which antibody is typically elevated after strep throat?
questions.explanation: ASO is the antibody against streptolysin O, produced by Streptococcus pyogenes, and is elevated in the majority of patients with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis after pharyngitis.

questions.question: What is the first-line treatment for acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: The initial treatment is to eradicate the streptococcus with penicillin, although glomerulonephritis is an immunological reaction; corticosteroids are not useful and cyclophosphamide is reserved for other vasculitis.

questions.question: What urinary finding is characteristic in the acute phase of this disease?
questions.explanation: Dysmorphic hematuria with red blood cell casts is typical of acute immune complex nephritis, indicating glomerular damage; glucosuria suggests tubulopathy and bacteriuria a urinary infection.

questions.question: What low complement level is typically seen in this glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: In poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, the alternate complement pathway is activated, predominantly consuming C3, while C4 is usually normal; This distinguishes it from other nephropathies.

questions.question: What is the average period between pharyngitis and the onset of nephritis?
questions.explanation: The typical latency period after strep throat is 1 to 3 weeks, unlike skin infection which can take longer; This information guides the diagnosis.

questions.question: Which antibody is most useful for confirming acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis after impetigo?
questions.explanation: After skin infections such as impetigo, the ASO response is weak, while anti-DNase B titers rise significantly and consistently, being the serological marker of choice.

questions.question: Why is anti-DNase B preferable to ASO in glomerulonephritis after impetigo?
questions.explanation: Streptococcal skin infections produce a poor humoral immune response against streptolysin O due to the presence of skin lipids that inhibit its antigen, making anti-DNase B the most reliable marker.

questions.question: What is the typical period of anti-DNase B elevation after streptococcal impetigo?
questions.explanation: Anti-DNase B antibodies peak between 3 and 6 weeks after skin infection, allowing confirmation of streptococcal etiology when requested in the acute phase of glomerulonephritis.

questions.question: In poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis due to impetigo, what serological finding supports the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Elevation of anti-DNase B is the key serological marker in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis secondary to skin infection, since ASO is usually normal or low in these cases, and C3 is typically decreased.

questions.question: What antibiotic treatment is indicated in a patient with acute glomerulonephritis and active impetigo?
questions.explanation: In poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, if there is evidence of active infection such as impetigo, benzathine penicillin is administered to eradicate the streptococcus; However, it does not modify the evolution of already established nephropathy.

questions.question: What acute complication should be monitored as a priority in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: High blood pressure is the most frequent and dangerous acute complication in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, due to volume expansion due to hydrosaline retention, and requires strict control to avoid hypertensive encephalopathy.

questions.question: What morphological characteristic defines dysmorphic hematuria in the urinary sediment?
questions.explanation: Dysmorphic hematuria is characterized by erythrocytes with altered morphology, such as acanthocytes and schistocytes, indicating glomerular origin. Normal erythrocytes suggest lower urinary tract bleeding.

questions.question: What is the main pathophysiological mechanism of glomerular hematuria in acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
options: Obstruction of the renal artery due to embolus
Acute tubular necrosis due to toxins
Deposit of immune complexes in the mesangium
questions.explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is a glomerulonephritis mediated by immune complexes that are deposited in the mesangium and basement membrane, activating complement and causing glomerular damage with hematuria.

questions.question: Which clinical finding is most suggestive of hematuria of glomerular origin in a patient with glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Glomerular hematuria typically presents dysmorphic erythrocytes and blood casts in the sediment, reflecting bleeding at the level of the glomerulus. Clots and initial hematuria suggest low urological origin.

questions.question: What color does the urine acquire in the choluric hematuria typical of acute glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Glomerular hematuria produces tea or Coca-Cola colored urine due to the oxidation of hemoglobin in the acidic environment, while lower urinary tract hematuria is usually bright red with clots.

questions.question: Which complementary test is most useful to confirm the glomerular origin of dysmorphic hematuria?
questions.explanation: Phase contrast microscopy of urinary sediment is the standard technique to identify erythrocyte dysmorphism, including acanthocytes, confirming glomerular origin of hematuria.

questions.question: What percentage of acanthocytes in the urinary sediment is considered highly specific for glomerular hematuria?
questions.explanation: The presence of more than 5% of acanthocytes (erythrocytes with ring-shaped projections) in the urinary sediment has high specificity for glomerular hematuria, being a widely used diagnostic criterion.

questions.question: What is the primary mechanism of hypertension in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Acute hypertension is due to sodium and water retention due to decreased glomerular filtration, expanding the extracellular volume. The other options are chronic secondary causes unrelated to the acute condition.

questions.question: Which finding is characteristic of edema in acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: The edema is typically periorbital and morning, due to hydrosaline retention and fluid redistribution during recumbency. The other options correspond to other mechanisms of edema or local causes.

questions.question: What is the first-line antihypertensive treatment in the hypertensive crisis of acute glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Intravenous furosemide is the initial treatment because it reduces blood volume, the main mechanism of hypertension in these patients. The other drugs do not act on volume expansion and may be less effective or risky in this context.

questions.question: What acute complication can develop if hypertension is not controlled in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Hypertensive encephalopathy is the most feared complication in children with acute glomerulonephritis, manifesting with seizures and altered state of consciousness. The other complications are more typical of chronic hypertension in adults.

questions.question: Which laboratory finding supports the diagnosis of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis in a patient with hypertension and edema?
questions.explanation: Elevated antistreptolysin O (ASO) and decreased complement C3 are typical of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. The other serological patterns correspond to vasculitis, lupus or cryoglobulinemia.

questions.question: What is the expected course of hypertension and edema in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis has a self-limiting course, with resolution of hypertension and edema in most pediatric patients within 2 to 6 weeks. The other options describe evolutions of other glomerulopathies.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of oliguria in acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Oliguria in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is due to a decrease in the glomerular filtration rate due to inflammation and cell proliferation in the glomeruli, reducing the excretion of water and solutes.

questions.question: Which laboratory finding is characteristic of oliguric acute renal failure?
questions.explanation: Hyperkalemia is a common complication of oliguric acute renal failure due to decreased renal potassium excretion, which can cause lethal arrhythmias.

questions.question: What is the first-line treatment for severe hyperkalemia in acute renal failure?
questions.explanation: Calcium gluconate stabilizes the cardiac membrane, protecting against arrhythmias, although it does not reduce serum potassium; It is the immediate treatment in an emergency.

questions.question: What cardiovascular complication is most feared in severe hyperkalemia?
questions.explanation: Severe hyperkalemia can cause fatal arrhythmias such as ventricular fibrillation or asystole; Membrane stabilization with calcium is crucial to prevent them.

questions.question: What is the main pathophysiological mechanism of oliguria in acute glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis induces inflammation and cell proliferation in the glomeruli, reducing the filtration surface and causing oliguria.

questions.question: What indication is required for dialysis in oliguric acute renal failure?
questions.explanation: Hyperkalemia refractory to medical treatment is an absolute indication for emergency dialysis, along with volume overload, severe acidosis, and symptomatic uremia.

questions.question: In which of the following situations of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is renal biopsy indicated?
options: Isolated microscopic hematuria that disappears in 2 weeks
Proteinuria in persistent nephrotic range at 6 weeks
Transient arterial hypotension during the acute phase
questions.explanation: La biopsia renal se indica cuando hay proteinuria en rango nefrótico que persiste más de 4-6 semanas, deterioro progresivo de la función renal o ausencia de recuperación esperada. La hematuria microscópica aislada y transitoria, la hipotensión pasajera y la elevación de ASO son hallazgos esperados que no requieren biopsia.

questions.question: ¿Qué hallazgo clínico constituye una indicación clásica de biopsia renal en la glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica?
options: Edema leve de miembros inferiores autolimitado
Deterioro rápido de la función renal oligúrica
questions.explanation: El deterioro rápido de la función renal con oliguria sugiere una evolución atípica o una glomerulonefritis rápidamente progresiva, por lo que la biopsia renal está indicada para confirmar el diagnóstico y guiar el tratamiento. La hematuria macroscópica recurrente sin proteinuria, la hipocomplementemia transitoria y el edema leve son hallazgos típicos que no requieren biopsia.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es la indicación más aceptada para realizar biopsia renal en un paciente con glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica?
options: Persistencia de proteinuria nefrótica después de 6 semanas
Appearance of mild arterial hypertension at the beginning
Descenso del complemento sérico a las dos semanas
questions.explanation: La proteinuria en rango nefrótico que persiste más de 6 semanas indica una evolución no típica y obliga a descartar otras glomerulopatías mediante biopsia renal. La hipocomplementemia inicial, la hipertensión leve transitoria y la hematuria con cilindros son manifestaciones esperadas de la enfermedad y no constituyen indicación de biopsia.

questions.question: ¿Qué hallazgo en la evolución de la glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica sugiere la necesidad de biopsia renal?
options: Normalización del complemento a las 8 semanas
Persistencia de hematuria microscópica a los 6 meses
Proteinuria de 3 gramos por día a los 4 meses
Hipertensión arterial controlada con un fármaco
questions.explanation: La proteinuria persistente en rango nefrótico (mayor de 3 g/día) después de 4-6 meses indica una evolución no resuelta y obliga a biopsia renal para evaluar daño glomerular crónico. La normalización del complemento, la hematuria microscópica residual y la hipertensión controlada son hallazgos compatibles con resolución típica.

questions.question: En la glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica, ¿cuándo se recomienda biopsia renal por sospecha de enfermedad rápidamente progresiva?
options: Cuando la creatinina sérica aumenta 30% en dos semanas
Cuando hay hematuria macroscópica inicial intensa
Si la proteinuria es de 1 gramo por día a los 3 meses
Si aparece anemia normocítica leve al mes
questions.explanation: Un aumento rápido de la creatinina sérica (30% o más en dos semanas) sugiere glomerulonefritis rápidamente progresiva, condición que requiere biopsia renal urgente para confirmar la presencia de semilunas y decidir tratamiento inmunosupresor. La anemia leve, la hematuria macroscópica inicial y la proteinuria subnefrótica no indican biopsia por sí solas.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es una indicación formal de biopsia renal en un niño con glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica?
options: Hipocomplementemia que persiste más de 8 semanas
Proteinuria de 500 mg/día que resuelve en 4 semanas
Hematuria macroscópica que dura más de 15 días
Hipertensión arterial que requiere dos fármacos al inicio
questions.explanation: La hipocomplementemia en la glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica se normaliza en 6-8 semanas; su persistencia más allá de 8 semanas sugiere otra glomerulopatía (como la membranoproliferativa) y obliga a biopsia renal. La hematuria macroscópica prolongada, la proteinuria subnefrótica transitoria y la hipertensión inicial que responde al tratamiento no son indicaciones de biopsia.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el pronóstico habitual de la glomerulonefritis aguda postestreptocócica en niños?
questions.explanation: En niños, la glomerulonefritis aguda postestreptocócica tiene un pronóstico excelente, con resolución espontánea en la mayoría de los casos y baja incidencia de progresión a enfermedad renal crónica.

questions.question: ¿Qué porcentaje aproximado de niños con glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica presenta recuperación completa?
questions.explanation: La recuperación completa ocurre en más del 95% de los niños con glomerulonefritis aguda postestreptocócica, lo que refleja su excelente pronóstico en la edad pediátrica.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es la complicación más temida en la fase aguda de la glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica infantil?
questions.explanation: La encefalopatía hipertensiva es una complicación aguda grave por hipertensión severa, aunque el pronóstico renal a largo plazo sigue siendo excelente en niños.

questions.question: ¿Qué hallazgo histológico es característico en la glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica infantil?
questions.explanation: Los depósitos subepiteliales en joroba son típicos de la glomerulonefritis aguda postestreptocócica, visibles en microscopía electrónica y asociados a buen pronóstico en niños.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el mecanismo fisiopatológico central de la glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica?
questions.explanation: La glomerulonefritis aguda postestreptocócica es mediada por inmunocomplejos que se depositan en el glomérulo, activando complemento y causando daño inflamatorio.

questions.question: ¿Qué tratamiento de soporte es esencial durante la fase aguda en niños con glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica?
options: Control de presión arterial y diuresis
questions.explanation: El manejo es de soporte: control de hipertensión, balance de líquidos y vigilancia de función renal, ya que la mayoría de niños se recupera espontáneamente sin necesidad de inmunosupresión.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es la indicación de antibiótico profiláctico en un paciente con glomerulonefritis aguda postestreptocócica?
options: Todos los pacientes con la infección
questions.explanation: La glomerulonefritis aguda postestreptocócica no requiere antibiótico profiláctico, a diferencia de la fiebre reumática aguda, donde se indica profilaxis secundaria. El tratamiento de la infección estreptocócica inicial es suficiente.

questions.question: ¿Qué medida es correcta en el manejo de la glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica?
questions.explanation: La glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica se maneja con tratamiento sintomático (control de hipertensión, edema y complicaciones) y no requiere profilaxis antibiótica prolongada, ya que el daño renal es inmunomediado y no por infección persistente.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es la conducta antibiótica ante un paciente con glomerulonefritis aguda postestreptocócica y cultivo faríngeo positivo?
questions.explanation: Si el cultivo es positivo, se debe tratar la infección estreptocócica activa con el antibiótico adecuado (penicilina) para erradicar el microorganismo, pero no se indica profilaxis prolongada porque no previene la nefritis.

questions.question: ¿En qué situación se podría considerar profilaxis antibiótica en un paciente con antecedente de glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica?
questions.explanation: La profilaxis antibiótica prolongada está indicada solo en fiebre reumática aguda, no en glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica. Si el paciente desarrolla fiebre reumática, se administra profilaxis secundaria, pero no por la nefritis.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el fundamento para no usar profilaxis antibiótica en la glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica?
questions.explanation: La glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica es una complicación inmunomediada que ocurre semanas después de la infección, por lo que la profilaxis antibiótica no previene el daño renal, a diferencia de la fiebre reumática.

questions.question: ¿Qué antibiótico profiláctico se administra a un paciente con glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica que no tiene infección activa?
questions.explanation: No se administra profilaxis antibiótica en glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica porque no hay infección activa ni riesgo de recurrencia; el manejo se centra en controlar la hipertensión y el edema.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el diurético de elección inicial en la glomerulonefritis aguda postestreptocócica con edema e hipertensión?
questions.explanation: La furosemida es el diurético de elección en la glomerulonefritis aguda postestreptocócica cuando hay edema e hipertensión, ya que es un diurético de asa potente que reduce la volemia y mejora la congestión. La espironolactona está contraindicada por riesgo de hiperpotasemia, y la hidroclorotiazida es menos efectiva en la insuficiencia renal aguda.

questions.question: ¿Qué parámetro se debe vigilar estrictamente al usar diuréticos de asa en esta enfermedad?
questions.explanation: En la glomerulonefritis aguda postestreptocócica existe tendencia a la hiperpotasemia por la disminución de la tasa de filtración glomerular; el uso de diuréticos de asa puede causar hipopotasemia, por lo que se debe vigilar el potasio sérico. El sodio urinario no es el parámetro de vigilancia principal, y el calcio o magnesio son menos relevantes.

questions.question: En la glomerulonefritis aguda postestreptocócica, ¿qué medida sintomática está indicada para controlar la hipertensión arterial?
options: Immediate start ACEI or ARA II
questions.explanation: El tratamiento inicial de la hipertensión en la glomerulonefritis aguda postestreptocócica incluye restricción de sodio y diuréticos de asa para reducir la volemia. Los IECA o ARA II pueden empeorar la hiperpotasemia y la lesión renal aguda, por lo que se evitan en la fase aguda. Los bloqueadores beta o calcioantagonistas no son la primera línea sintomática.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es la principal indicación para usar diuréticos en la glomerulonefritis aguda postestreptocócica?
questions.explanation: La indicación principal de los diuréticos en esta glomerulonefritis es la presencia de edema pulmonar o congestión sistémica significativa. La hiperpotasemia y la hipertensión se tratan con otras medidas, y la proteinuria no es indicación directa de diurético. El edema pulmonar requiere reducir la precarga con diuréticos de asa.

questions.question: ¿Qué complicación electrolítica se previene al evitar diuréticos ahorradores de potasio en este cuadro?
questions.explanation: En la glomerulonefritis aguda postestreptocócica existe un estado de hiperpotasemia debido a la insuficiencia renal; los diuréticos ahorradores de potasio (como espironolactona) aumentarían aún más el potasio, predisponiendo a arritmias. Por ello se deben evitar. La hiponatremia, hipocalcemia o hipermagnesemia no son el riesgo principal.

questions.question: ¿Qué tratamiento sintomático se recomienda para el edema leve sin hipertensión en esta patología?
options: Reposo relativo y restricción de sodio
questions.explanation: En el edema leve sin hipertensión en la glomerulonefritis aguda postestreptocócica se recomienda reposo relativo y restricción de sodio, evitando diuréticos agresivos. Los diuréticos de asa intravenosos se reservan para edema severo o congestión. Los diuréticos osmóticos están contraindicados y los expansores de plasma empeoran la sobrecarga.
